Maladaptive Strategies.value: I push myself to exercise excessively

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

issues.item: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: The trauma type is trauma to a loved one, but this maladaptive strategy presumes a direct perpetrator who harmed the patient. That is hard to reconcile unless the loved one's trauma also directly involved interpersonal harm to the patient, which is not indicated here.

issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: Permanent humiliation is more characteristic of direct interpersonal victimization. With a loved-one trauma, this appraisal is not impossible, but in combination with 'others can see what happened to me' it implies a self-referential shame exposure theme that fits poorly unless the patient was also directly victimized.

vignette:
Aroha Ngata is a fifty-seven-year-old Māori woman, divorced, who works as a senior architect at a mid-sized firm in Seattle. She was referred for psychological assessment following a brief conversation with her general practitioner, whom she had visited for a stress-related complaint - the first medical appointment she had kept in nearly two years. Her PCL-5 score of 70 places her in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across the intake and first two sessions is one of a woman whose interior world has been quietly collapsing for some time, even as her professional output has remained, on the surface, intact.

The precipitating event occurred approximately twenty-six months ago, when Aroha's adult daughter, Mia, suffered a catastrophic allergic reaction at a family gathering and was rushed by ambulance to the emergency department. Aroha was present throughout - she rode in the ambulance, she stood in the corridor while staff worked, and she sat for hours in a waiting room that smelled sharply of antiseptic and floor cleaner, listening to the incomprehensible rapid-fire exchanges between clinicians calling across the unit. Mia survived, but the hours before that outcome were ones in which Aroha was entirely certain her daughter was dying. The sounds of that corridor - urgent, clipped, unintelligible - and the chemical smell of the hospital have since become the clearest channels back into that certainty.

In the weeks after Mia's discharge, Aroha found that certain spaces activated something she could not name or contain. The hospital smell, reproduced faintly in any clinical environment, would arrive before she had consciously registered it, and the sensation that followed was less memory than re-immersion. Incomprehensible background chatter - overheard conversations in open-plan offices, the murmur of a television in a waiting room - produced the same flooding. Physical locations associated with that day, including the hospital district and, more troublingly, the street near the family home where the ambulance had been called, became unbearable. As these triggers multiplied and intensified, Aroha began organising her life around them. She stopped attending the medical appointments her GP had recommended. She rerouted her commute. She declined social invitations, telling herself she was simply busy, and then stopped telling herself anything at all - she simply stopped going. What she did instead was exercise: long runs before dawn, punishing gym sessions after work, a physical exhaustion she pursued with the focused determination she had once given to design projects. The exercise quieted the intrusive activation, at least temporarily, and so it became the architecture of her evenings.

The consequences of these strategies accumulated in ways she had not anticipated. Withdrawing from friends meant that her understanding of herself went uncontested and untested. She had come to believe, with a quiet but absolute conviction, that something was visible on her face - that colleagues and acquaintances could see the event written into her expression, that she was legible in a way she found intolerable. Staying away from people protected her from that exposure, but it also meant the belief was never challenged. The avoidance of medical cues, which had begun as a practical strategy, deepened her sense that the world was a place of unmanageable danger, and with it her faith - in people, in the structures of ordinary life, in whatever had once given her days a sense of forward motion - continued to erode. Nothing in her work felt meaningful in the way it once had; she produced drawings and attended meetings and met deadlines, but the connective tissue between effort and significance had gone slack. These appraisals, in turn, made the triggers more potent: when she believed she was permanently marked and that nothing mattered, a hospital smell was not just an unpleasant sensation but confirmation of a ruined world, and the flooding that followed drove her back to avoidance and the pre-dawn runs.

By the time she arrived at her GP's office, Aroha had not seen most of her close friends in over a year. A former colleague had recently asked, gently, whether she was all right, and something in the question had broken through. She came to therapy, she said, because she was exhausted - not from the running, but from the management of it all. What she most feared was that this was simply who she was now. What she most hoped, though she offered it quietly and without much conviction, was that it might not be permanent.
